title: The octopus problem
text: Of all the puzzles in the sea, the octopus may be the most {{1}}: a mollusc, related to clams and snails, that behaves like something from another planet. It has no bones, so it can {{2}} through an opening the size of its eyeball, and colour cells in its skin let it match the seabed in under a second — despite being, as far as we can tell, completely colour-blind. The real mystery is its intelligence. Two thirds of its neurons sit not in the brain but along the arms, and each arm can {{3}} problems — tasting, gripping, exploring — with an independence that makes the animal less a single mind than a {{4}} of cooperating specialists. In laboratories octopuses unscrew jars from the inside, remember individual keepers and squirt water at the ones they {{5}}. One resident made a hobby of {{6}} its tank lamp with jets of water until the bulb shorted, less out of malice, researchers suspect, than a preference for the {{7}}. The animal is now taken seriously enough that EU welfare rules {{8}} anaesthetic for octopus surgery — protection once reserved for creatures with backbones.

gaps.explanation: 'the most intriguing puzzle' — fascinating because strange; intimate = close, intrusive = unwelcome, inert = motionless.
'squeeze through an opening' — push the soft body through; swallow goes one way only, and scatter breaks the meaning.
'each arm can solve problems' — work them out; the -volve forms share a shape but not the meaning.
'a committee of cooperating specialists' — a group acting together; comment, commerce and commodity are abstract nouns that cannot cooperate.
'the ones they dislike' — have taken against personally; dismiss = send away, dispose takes 'of'.
'soaking its tank lamp with jets of water' — drenching it; seep is intransitive and sip is for drinks.
'a preference for the dark' — 'the dark' is the fixed noun for darkness; dull describes light quality, not a place.
'welfare rules require anaesthetic' — make it necessary; inquire and enquire = ask, acquire = obtain.
